[PAPER_0013, relevance_score=0.329] Crucially, our explanation of the popularity bias leads to a novel prediction. If the relative size of review samples was attributed to factors other than product quality, then the bias toward choice of the more reviewed option should be reduced or eliminated. The current experiments tested this prediction.

[PAPER_0015, relevance_score=0.271] Crucially, the explanation for the difference in review sample sizes was manipulated between groups. One group was given no reason for this difference. The other was given sample size explanations that were unrelated to product quality (e.g., the MRP had been on the market for a longer time). In the no explanation group, we expected to replicate the popularity bias reported by Powell et al.

(2017). When the difference in sample sizes was due to a cause unrelated to quality, we expected that the popularity bias would be substantially reduced.

[PAPER_0025, relevance_score=0.279] To test for such effects, linear and quadratic trend contrasts were planned for the MRP advantage factor. Our causal attribution account suggests an interaction between quadratic trend for MRP advantage and the explanation manipulation-a nonlinear pattern of ratings across levels of MRP advantage should be more evident in the no explanation than the explanation condition.

Across groups, there was a significant linear effect of MRP advantage on rated preference for the MRP, F(1, 285) = 514.86, p < .001, ηp2 = .644, with MRP preference increasing as its quality advantage increased.

[PAPER_0024, relevance_score=0.324] Results and Discussion

Preference Ratings

Figure 2 shows mean preference ratings for the more-reviewed product. These data were analyzed in a 2 (explanation) × 5 (mean review score of the MRP) × 5 (MRP advantage) mixed-model analysis of variance (ANOVA), with repeated measures on the last two factors. In the Powell et al. (2017) data, the effects of levels of MRP advantage on preference were nonlinear (negative advantage levels had more of an effect on ratings than positive advantage levels).

[PAPER_0025, relevance_score=0.306] To test for such effects, linear and quadratic trend contrasts were planned for the MRP advantage factor. Our causal attribution account suggests an interaction between quadratic trend for MRP advantage and the explanation manipulation-a nonlinear pattern of ratings across levels of MRP advantage should be more evident in the no explanation than the explanation condition.

Across groups, there was a significant linear effect of MRP advantage on rated preference for the MRP, F(1, 285) = 514.86, p < .001, ηp2 = .644, with MRP preference increasing as its quality advantage increased.

[PAPER_0026, relevance_score=0.285] Across groups, there was also a significant quadratic trend effect of MRP advantage on preference ratings, F(1, 285) = 129.49, p < .001, ηp2 = .312, similar to that observed in the Powell et al. data. There was also a main effect of MRP score, F(1, 285) = 92.451, p < .001, ηp2 = .245, reflecting increasing preference for the MRP as its quality score increased.

[PAPER_0029, relevance_score=0.287] In contrast, in the explanation group, preference for the more reviewed product was more dependent on the MRP advantage in quality scores. These group differences were reflected in a significant interaction between group and quadratic trend for MRP advantage, F(1, 285) = 8.71, p = .003, ηp2 = .03.

(N.B. Complementary multilevel regression analyses for both experiments were carried out. These analyses replicated all of the key effects reported here; see https://osf.io/5gbsv/).

[PAPER_0031, relevance_score=0.375] Modeling

We fitted the Bayesian "intuitive statistician" model developed by Powell et al. (2017) to dichotomized ratings data. This model calculates a posterior estimate of the true mean quality value (θ) of a product, given a sample quality mean (x), with standard deviation (S) and the size of the sample (n; see Powell et al., 2017 for computational details). Powell et al. (2017) estimated parameter values from a database of over 70,000 Amazon reviews of cell phone accessories so there are no free parameters.1

[PAPER_0032, relevance_score=0.413] Figure 3 shows the relationship between model predictions and choice data for target trials. We examined whether sample size explanation affected model fit by entering the intuitive statistician model predictions and group membership as predictors in a Bayesian linear regression (cf. Rouder & Morey, 2012) with observed choice data from both groups as the dependent measure. A regression model including both explanation group and model predictors provided a better fit to the data (R2 = .82) than a regression model without the group factor (R2 = .72), BF10 = 2311.33.

[PAPER_0024, relevance_score=0.201] Results and Discussion

Preference Ratings

Figure 2 shows mean preference ratings for the more-reviewed product. These data were analyzed in a 2 (explanation) × 5 (mean review score of the MRP) × 5 (MRP advantage) mixed-model analysis of variance (ANOVA), with repeated measures on the last two factors. In the Powell et al. (2017) data, the effects of levels of MRP advantage on preference were nonlinear (negative advantage levels had more of an effect on ratings than positive advantage levels).

[PAPER_0031, relevance_score=0.228] Modeling

We fitted the Bayesian "intuitive statistician" model developed by Powell et al. (2017) to dichotomized ratings data. This model calculates a posterior estimate of the true mean quality value (θ) of a product, given a sample quality mean (x), with standard deviation (S) and the size of the sample (n; see Powell et al., 2017 for computational details). Powell et al. (2017) estimated parameter values from a database of over 70,000 Amazon reviews of cell phone accessories so there are no free parameters.1

[PAPER_0016, relevance_score=0.310] Method

Participants

A total of 303 participants (Mage = 35.79, SD = 9.41; 202 males, 100 females, one nonbinary) were recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) and paid U.S. $2.00. Sixteen were excluded for failing attention checks. Remaining participants were randomly allocated to either a no explanation (n = 145) or explanation group (n = 142). Both Experiments 1 and 2 were approved by the UNSW Human Research Ethics Panel.

[PAPER_0020, relevance_score=0.291] Those who failed both items for either pair were excluded.

On each of the 33 trials, online review information was presented about two products described as "similarly-priced smartphone cases. Products were labeled by randomly generated letters. The mean quality score for each product was shown by number of stars and a numerical value out of 5. The number of reviews on which scores were based appeared beside the quality score. Participants rated their product preference on a 6-point scale (see Figure 1). Left-right position of the MRP was counterbalanced across trials.

[PAPER_0024, relevance_score=0.260] Results and Discussion

Preference Ratings

Figure 2 shows mean preference ratings for the more-reviewed product. These data were analyzed in a 2 (explanation) × 5 (mean review score of the MRP) × 5 (MRP advantage) mixed-model analysis of variance (ANOVA), with repeated measures on the last two factors. In the Powell et al. (2017) data, the effects of levels of MRP advantage on preference were nonlinear (negative advantage levels had more of an effect on ratings than positive advantage levels).
